Mathematics Education · Miami University

Start where you are.
Build backward, then forward.

A template for students who join the program in Year 3. One semester reconstructs the baseline from work you already have; the last three semesters run the full cycle.

Template · Transfer students and juniors declaring math education

Selection. Reflection. Connection.

Definition 1.1 (ePortfolio). A curated collection of student-created work — for learning, assessment, and showcase — with reflection on each artifact and on the connections between them.

Corollary (Math Ed Portfolio). The same thing, organized around what a beginning mathematics teacher needs to be able to do. Without reflection it is a repository. With it, it is the argument, with evidence, that you are ready for your own classroom.

Principles for a late startSlide 02

Reconstruct honestly. Then run the same cycle as everyone else.

The four learning features don't change. What changes is that the first versions are written looking back rather than looking forward.

Reconstruct, don't fabricate

Your Year 1 baseline is a retrospective: who you were when you arrived at college, written now, with the date. Old work from other courses or institutions counts as artifacts.

Retrospective reflection is still reflection

Prompts ask what you thought then and what you think now, so the first entry already contains a change — the thing the portfolio is designed to show.

Compressed cycle, same moves

Letters, philosophy versions, goal check-ins, and feedback replies happen each semester instead of each year.

Same site, same pages

Your MILE shell and Math Ed pages match every other student's, so mentors and the Year 4 presentation work the same way.

MILE alignmentSlide 03

MILE requirements, compressed to four semesters

A late-start student still owes MILE the same pieces: About Me, Advanced Writing, three ASC artifacts, Capstone, and a concluding reflection. Check with MILO on what transfer credit already satisfies; everything else maps below.

Junior fallSlide 05

Reconstruct the baseline

You have more to work with than you think: transcripts, old assignments, tutoring or coaching experience, your own schooling. The job this semester is to turn that into a dated starting point.

What you add

  • Portfolio shell (MILE) Create the Google Site — or use the MILE shell from UNV 101 or its equivalent if you already have one. Write About Me; add the Math Ed section with pages for each semester.
  • Retrospective letter Two parts, both dated now: who you were when you started college and what you believed about teaching; who you are today and who you want to become.
  • Teaching philosophy v1 Written from your best memory of what you believed two years ago. Keep it honest; it is supposed to look dated.
  • Two artifacts from prior work A piece of your own mathematics (a Quantitative Reasoning ASC artifact if the course qualifies) and anything teaching-adjacent — a tutoring log, a lesson from another program.

What keeps learning going

  • Then / now prompts Every retrospective reflection has two columns: what I thought then, what I think now. The gap is the first evidence of growth.
  • Dated versions from day one philosophy-F27-retro, philosophy-S28. Never overwrite.
  • Mentor intake conversation Your mentor reads the retrospective letter and asks one question you answer on the page.
  • Muddiest point One sentence: what about teaching math is least clear to you right now?
Reflection promptWhat did you believe about learning mathematics when you started college? Point to something you wrote or did then that shows it.
Junior springSlide 06

Teach and analyze

With the baseline in place, the semester runs the Year 3 template: real students, real work, real feedback.

What you add

  • Second lesson plan Different grade band or strand than the fall plan.
  • Analysis of student work Anonymized responses to a task you gave, sorted by strategy and misconception, with what you'd do next.
  • Assessment you designed A quiz, task, or rubric, plus results and what they told you.
  • Teaching philosophy v2 Rewritten, with a note on what changed since the retrospective v1 — and what caused it.

What keeps learning going

  • Compare plan to plan Fall and spring lesson plans side by side. Name three differences and what they show.
  • Feedback log with replies Methods instructor and cooperating teacher feedback, each with a reply within a week.
  • Answer the muddiest point Return to the fall question; ask the next.
  • Peer read Trade portfolios with a classmate who started in Year 1. Each leaves one comment the other must answer.
Reflection promptFind a student response that surprised you. What did the student understand that your plan didn't anticipate?
Senior yearSlide 07

Placement depth, then the argument

Senior fall deepens the placement evidence; senior spring turns the record into a presentation, exactly as in the Four-Year Build.

What you add

  • Lesson wrapper (fall) After teaching: how you prepared, where students struggled, what you'll do differently.
  • Teaching philosophy v3 and v4 v3 with every claim linked to an artifact; v4 presented beside the retrospective v1.
  • Classroom video with commentary (spring) 10–15 minutes with time-stamped notes on your questions and decisions.
  • Growth record & concluding reflection (MILE) Every logged piece of feedback with its response; the MILE concluding reflection plus a program reflection. Submit the link via MILO's form in Capstone.

What keeps learning going

  • Integration reflection Referencing artifacts from all four semesters — including the reconstructed ones — what can you do now that you couldn't?
  • Reread every letter Retrospective, junior spring, senior fall. Write the last: to yourself at the end of your first year teaching.
  • Portfolio presentation Present to faculty and peers; reply to their feedback as the final growth-record entry.
  • Hand-off Submit the MILE link to MILO. Remove instructors' access. Keep the site.
Reflection promptYour retrospective letter guessed who you would become. Where was it right, where was it wrong, and what does the portfolio show about why?

Using this templateSlide 09

What the program needs for late-start students

Most of it is shared with the Four-Year Build. Three pieces are specific to reconstruction.

1

Retrospective letter prompt

Two-part, then/now. This is the one document a late-start student cannot borrow from the standard template.

2

Prior-work intake checklist

What counts as an artifact from another institution or a non-education course, how to reflect on it retrospectively, and which MILE requirements MILO counts as satisfied by transfer credit.

3

Mentor intake conversation guide

One meeting, one question logged on the page. Sets the feedback-reply norm from the first week.

4

Semester-cadence calendar

The same five recurring features, mapped to four semesters instead of four years.

5

Shared everything else

Artifact page template, reflection rubric, and Year 4 presentation format are identical to the Four-Year Build.

Sources: Miami ePortfolios Working Group, F'26 · Perkins & Salomon on transfer · Schraw (1998) · Tanner (2012)
